item.description:
Normalisation not discussed during months of Saudi-US nuclear negotiations, sources say

Since November 2025, the US and Saudi Arabia have been hashing out a civilian nuclear agreement, but in dozens of exchanges between officials, Riyadh’s diplomatic recognition of Israel never once came up, one current and one former US official familiar with the talks told Middle East Eye.

“Normalisation was never listed as a condition,” one of the sources told MEE. “Not once.”

Less than 24 hours after Saudi Arabia and the US signed a nuclear deal on Wednesday, President Donald Trump declared the agreement “totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords”.

The social media post likely blindsided US and Arab officials, not least because Trump and Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had just spoken that day. The two countries’ top diplomats also held a phone call on Wednesday.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] The Karim Khan saga: a timeline
item.description:
The Karim Khan saga: a timeline

Member states of the International Criminal Court (ICC) are due to vote at the United Nations' headquarters in New York on Friday on whether to remove the court's chief prosecutor, Karim Khan, from office – a first in the court’s 24-year history. 

The vote caps a saga stretching back more than two years, spanning sexual misconduct allegations Khan has consistently denied, a UN-led investigation, a judicial panel that unanimously cleared him, and a bureau that chose to override that finding and press ahead regardless.

The case has unfolded alongside a separate campaign of pressure on Khan and the court over his pursuit of war crimes warrants against Israeli and Hamas leaders, from a threat by Britain's then foreign secretary to defund the ICC, to sanctions imposed on Khan and dozens of ICC officials by the Trump administration, to the US secretary of state's public vow to "dismantle" the court.

Khan, a British barrister, is the ICC's third chief prosecutor since the court’s founding in 2002. 

Read more: The Karim Khan saga: a timeline

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Eight Muslim countries condemn mass Israeli raid on Al-Aqsa
item.description:
Eight Muslim countries condemn mass Israeli raid on Al-Aqsa

Submitted by Mera Aladam on Fri, 07/24/2026 - 01:22
The statement follows a mass raid on the holy site by thousands of ultranationalist Israelis on Thursday
Israel's Minister of National Security Itamar Ben Gvir, amongst other officials, leading a mass ultranationalist raid on Al-Aqsa Mosque, in occupied East Jerusalem, on 23 July, 2026 (Reuters)
Off

The foreign ministers of Qatar, the UAE, Jordan, Turkey, Egypt, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia have denounced recent Israeli settler incursions at Jerusalem's Al-Aqsa Mosque as "illegal and extremist acts".

In a statement posted by Qatar's foreign ministry on X on Thursday, the ministers stressed that the storming of the holy sites constitute a "flagrant violation of international law, relevant United Nations resolutions, and the historic and legal status quo at the holy sites in Occupied East Jerusalem".

"The ministers condemned in the strongest terms, in a joint statement, the illegal and extremist acts represented by incitement and calls to mobilise incursions, as well as acts of violence committed by Israeli ministers and extremist groups," they added. 

They warned that such acts "fuel hatred and extremism, and obstruct efforts aimed at achieving a just and lasting peace based on the two-state solution", and urged the recognition of Jordan's historic custodianship of the Al-Aqsa complex.

The officials also rejected Israel's claim over the Occupied East Jerusalem and its Islamic and Christian holy sites as well as its attempt at to altering the "historical, legal, and demographic character" of the area. 

The statement follows a mass raid on Al-Aqsa Mosque by thousands of ultranationalist Israelis on Thursday, that was led by prominent ministers and lawmakers. 

Among those taking part were Itamar Ben Gvir, Israel's national security minister; Yitzhak Wasserlauf, minister for the Negev, Galilee and national resilience; and Amit Halevi, a lawmaker from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party.

Ahead of the raids, Israeli forces barred many Palestinians from reaching Al-Aqsa Mosque for pre-dawn prayers, forcing them to pray in nearby streets.

Al-Aqsa Mosque has been governed under a decades-long status quo, or international arrangement, preserving its religious status as an exclusively Islamic site.

Israeli ministers lead mass Al-Aqsa Mosque raid
Read More »

Under arrangements reached after the 1967 war, Jordan and Israel agreed that the Islamic Waqf would administer internal affairs at the complex, while Israel would control external security.

Non-Muslims are permitted to visit the site during designated hours, but are not allowed to pray there.

The mosque has seen escalating settler raids in recent years, often conducted under military escort.

Middle East Eye previously reported that the US and Israel are "actively working" to strip Jordan of its historic custodianship of Jerusalem's Al-Aqsa Mosque complex.

Under the proposed arrangement, revealed by MEE sources, management of the revered Muslim site will closely align with Israeli interests in the future.

US, Jordanian and Palestinian officials, as well as western and Gulf Arab sources, told MEE that under the plan, championed by Jared Kushner and US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, the authority of the Jordanian-backed Islamic Waqf would end and a new body created by the Israeli government would declare the Al-Aqsa Mosque a "multi-faith centre".

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that this was the case, but did not affirm Jordan's custodianship.

Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan said Ambassador Muhammad Shahrul Ikram Yaakob told the State Department that the country's longstanding policy of not recognising Israel was not new.

"It has always been Malaysia's policy. Our immigration policy does not recognise the State of Israel or the Zionist regime. This has long been our position," he said. 

"There was an individual with dual citizenship, the U.S. and Israel, who entered Malaysia using his U.S. passport. However, subsequent checks revealed that he also held Israeli citizenship, and we asked him to leave."

This comes after Malaysia prime minister Anwar Ibrahim's announcement last week indicating that authorities will deport any Israeli nationals found in the country.  

Malaysia’s Ministry of Home Affairs opened an investigation into a project called Network School after users on social media alleged that some participants were Israeli citizens with dual nationality who had entered Malaysia using passports from other countries - in violation of Kuala Lumpur's immigration laws.

Follow today’s news live

Australian exports sent to the US will be hit with a 12.5% tariff as the US president imposes levies on more than 80 nations.

The Trump administration unveiled the latest tranche of tariffs for countries over their “failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labour”.

This, in our view, makes no sense.

Forced labour is definitely something which needs to be combated around the world, so we support that objective.

We absolutely need to see the strait of Hormuz be open and for freedom of navigation to happen there, for commercial shipping to be allowed through, and we very much call on Iran to allow that to be the case.

We need to see a restoration to the normal global fuel supply chain because it’s having a significant impact around the world.
